exercises.name: Foam Roll Calves
instructions: Sit on the floor with the roller under one calf and your hands behind you.
Lift your hips slightly so your weight rests on the roller.
Roll slowly from just below the knee toward the ankle, pausing on tender spots.
Work for one to two minutes, then switch legs.
exercises.formCue: Slow and steady. Breathe on the tender spots.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rolling fast back and forth, or pressing so hard you tense up.
exercises.beginnerModification: Keep your hips on the floor and both feet relaxed to reduce the pressure.
exercises.whyThisMatters: A couple of minutes of slow rolling can ease the feeling of tight calves before or after training.

exercises.name: Foam Roll Quads
instructions: Lie face down on your forearms with the roller under the front of one thigh.
Keep your trunk braced so your lower back does not sag.
Roll slowly between the top of the knee and the hip crease.
Stop on a tender spot for 30 to 45 seconds, then move on and switch legs.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rolling over the kneecap, or holding your breath against the pressure.
exercises.beginnerModification: Roll both thighs at once to spread your weight.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It is a simple way to ease stiff quads around training.

source.name: NASM, Foam Rolling and Self-Myofascial Release: The Trainer's Application Guide

exercises.name: Foam Roll Outer Thigh
instructions: Lie on your side with the roller under the outer thigh, just below the hip.
Cross the top leg over and place that foot on the floor to take some weight.
Roll slowly along the outer thigh, stopping above the knee.
Keep the pressure moderate, pause briefly on tender areas, then switch sides.
exercises.formCue: Use the top foot to take weight off.
exercises.commonMistakes: Grinding hard on the side of the knee or the hip bone.
exercises.beginnerModification: Put more weight through the supporting foot and hand, or use a softer roller.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Gentle work on the muscles of the outer thigh can make the hip and knee feel freer.

source.name: NASM, Foam Rolling and Self-Myofascial Release: The Trainer's Application Guide

exercises.name: Foam Roll Glutes
instructions: Sit on the roller with your hands on the floor behind you.
Cross one ankle over the opposite knee and lean toward the hip of the crossed leg.
Roll slowly over the back of that hip to find a tender spot.
Hold there for 30 to 45 seconds while breathing normally, then switch sides.
exercises.formCue: Lean in, find the spot, breathe.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rolling quickly, or pressing into pain that shoots down the leg.
exercises.beginnerModification: Keep both feet on the floor and do not cross the leg.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It gives the back of the hip some relief after long sitting or heavy leg work.

source.name: NASM, Foam Rolling and Self-Myofascial Release: The Trainer's Application Guide

exercises.name: Foam Roll Upper Back
exercises.musclesWorked: Thoracic spine muscles, rhomboids, mid traps
instructions: Lie on your back with the roller across your mid back, knees bent and feet flat.
Support your head with your hands and lift your hips slightly.
Use your feet to roll slowly between the bottom of the shoulder blades and the top of the shoulders.
Pause at a stiff segment and gently ease back over the roller as you breathe out.
exercises.formCue: Ribs down, roll the upper back only.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rolling onto the lower back or neck, or flaring the ribs to force the arch.
exercises.beginnerModification: Keep your hips on the floor and just lean back over the roller without rolling.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It is a useful reset for an upper back that has been bent over a desk.

source.name: NASM, Foam Rolling and Self-Myofascial Release: The Trainer's Application Guide

exercises.name: Foam Roll Lats
instructions: Lie on your side with the roller just below your armpit and the bottom arm reaching overhead.
Use your top hand and feet on the floor for support.
Roll slowly from the armpit toward the lower ribs.
Pause on tight spots, work for one to two minutes, then switch sides.
exercises.commonMistakes: Too much pressure, or rolling onto the ribs at the front.
exercises.beginnerModification: Do it standing with the roller or a ball against a wall.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Easing the lats can make reaching overhead feel smoother.

exercises.name: Foam Roll Adductors
instructions: Lie face down on your forearms with one knee bent out to the side.
Place the roller under the inner thigh of that leg, at a right angle to it.
Roll slowly between the groin and the inside of the knee.
Pause on tender spots, work for one to two minutes, then switch legs.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rolling too fast or pressing right into the groin crease.
exercises.beginnerModification: Take more weight on your forearms and the other leg.
exercises.whyThisMatters: The inner thigh is easy to forget and often feels tight after squats and side-to-side work.

exercises.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent and your head supported.
Rest one hand on your upper chest and the other just below your ribs.
Breathe in slowly through your nose so the lower hand rises while the chest hand stays still.
Breathe out slowly through pursed lips as your belly falls, and repeat for a few minutes.
exercises.commonMistakes: Lifting the chest and shoulders, or forcing big breaths.
exercises.beginnerModification: Practise for one minute at a time and build up.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Slow belly breathing is a simple way to bring effort and heart rate down after training.

exercises.name: Box Breathing
instructions: Sit or lie comfortably and breathe all the way out.
Breathe in through your nose for a count of four.
Hold gently for a count of four.
Breathe out for a count of four, hold for four, and repeat for three or four rounds.
exercises.formCue: Four in, four hold, four out, four hold.
exercises.commonMistakes: Straining on the holds or counting too slowly for comfort.
exercises.beginnerModification: Use a count of three, or skip the holds.
exercises.whyThisMatters: An even counted breath gives the mind one simple thing to follow while the body settles.

exercises.name: Band External Rotation
instructions: Anchor a light band at elbow height and stand side-on to it.
Hold the band in the far hand with the elbow bent to 90 degrees and tucked to your side.
Rotate the forearm outward, keeping the elbow against your ribs.
Pause, then return slowly to the start.
exercises.commonMistakes: Letting the elbow drift away from the body, or using a band that is too heavy.
exercises.beginnerModification: Do it without a band, or lying on your side with a very light weight.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It strengthens the small rotator cuff muscles that keep the shoulder steady.

source.name: AAOS OrthoInfo, Rotator Cuff and Shoulder Conditioning Program

exercises.name: Shoulder Pendulum
instructions: Lean forward with one hand resting on a table.
Let the other arm hang straight down and relaxed.
Gently swing the arm forward and back, then side to side.
Finish with small circles in each direction, then switch arms.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rounding the back or using shoulder muscles to drive a big swing.
exercises.beginnerModification: Make the swings smaller.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It is a gentle way to move the shoulder without loading it.

source.name: AAOS OrthoInfo, Rotator Cuff and Shoulder Conditioning Program

exercises.name: Single-Leg Stand
instructions: Stand facing a wall with your fingertips resting on it.
Lift one foot off the floor, keeping your hips level.
Keep a slight bend in the standing knee and hold for 5 to 10 seconds.
Lower the foot and repeat on the other side.
exercises.formCue: Hips level, soft knee, eyes forward.
exercises.commonMistakes: Leaning the trunk to the side or locking the standing knee.
exercises.beginnerModification: Keep the toes of the lifted foot resting lightly on the floor.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Standing steady on one leg is the base of walking, stairs and catching yourself from a trip.

exercises.name: Tandem Stance
instructions: Stand tall beside a support.
Place one foot directly in front of the other so the heel touches the toes.
Look ahead and hold the position for 10 seconds.
Switch the front foot and repeat.
exercises.formCue: Feet on a tightrope, eyes up.
exercises.commonMistakes: Looking down at the feet or gripping the support hard.
exercises.beginnerModification: Leave a small gap between the feet, or stand with them slightly offset.
exercises.whyThisMatters: A narrow stance trains side-to-side steadiness with very little risk.

source.name: Otago Exercise Programme (Royal Orthopaedic Hospital NHS)

exercises.name: Heel-to-Toe Walk
instructions: Stand tall next to a wall.
Place one heel on the floor directly in front of the toes of the other foot.
Step the back foot through and place it heel to toe in front.
Keep looking forward and take at least five steps.
exercises.formCue: Look ahead, not at your feet.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rushing the steps or stepping wide to stay balanced.
exercises.beginnerModification: Run your fingers along the wall as you walk.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It trains the narrow-base balance needed for steady walking.

exercises.name: Sideways Walk
instructions: Stand with feet together and knees slightly bent.
Step one foot out to the side in a slow, controlled way.
Bring the other foot in to join it without dropping your hips.
Take 10 steps one way, then 10 steps back.
exercises.commonMistakes: Swaying the trunk or letting the feet turn out.
exercises.beginnerModification: Do it facing a kitchen counter with your hands resting on it.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Controlled side steps strengthen the hips that keep you steady when you move sideways.

exercises.name: Sit-to-Stand
instructions: Sit toward the front of a chair with feet hip-width apart.
Lean slightly forward, looking straight ahead.
Stand up slowly using your legs rather than your arms.
Stand fully upright, then sit back down slowly.
exercises.commonMistakes: Dropping back into the chair or pushing mostly with the hands.
exercises.beginnerModification: Use a higher seat or push lightly on the armrests.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Getting out of a chair without help is a basic test of leg strength for daily life.

exercises.name: Supported Mini Squat
instructions: Stand behind a chair with your hands resting on it and feet hip-width apart.
Bend your knees a comfortable amount, keeping them over your toes.
Keep your back straight and heels down.
Stand back up by squeezing your buttocks, and repeat.
exercises.commonMistakes: Leaning forward onto the chair or letting the knees fall inward.
exercises.beginnerModification: Bend only a few centimetres.
exercises.whyThisMatters: A short-range squat builds leg strength with support close at hand.

exercises.name: Supported Heel Raise
instructions: Stand tall with your hands resting on the back of a chair.
Lift both heels off the floor as far as is comfortable.
Move slowly and stay upright without leaning forward.
Lower the heels with control and repeat.
exercises.commonMistakes: Bouncing, or rolling out onto the outer edges of the feet.
exercises.beginnerModification: Do it seated, lifting the heels one at a time.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Strong calves help with walking, stairs and balance.

exercises.name: Low Step-Up
exercises.equipment: Low step with a rail or wall
instructions: Stand facing a low step with a hand on a rail or wall.
Step up with one foot and place the whole foot on the step.
Bring the other foot up to join it.
Step back down slowly, one foot at a time, and repeat leading with the other leg.
exercises.formCue: Whole foot on the step. Slow on the way down.
exercises.commonMistakes: Pulling up with the arm or dropping down quickly.
exercises.beginnerModification: Use a lower step and keep a firm hold of the rail.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It practises stair climbing in a controlled way.

exercises.name: Marching in Place
instructions: Stand tall with elbows bent and hands relaxed.
March on the spot, lifting each knee to a comfortable height.
Swing your arms in time with your steps.
Add a few steps forward and back as you keep the rhythm.
exercises.commonMistakes: Stamping the feet or slouching.
exercises.beginnerModification: Hold a support and lift the knees only a little.
exercises.whyThisMatters: A few minutes of marching raises body temperature gently before exercise.

source.name: NHS, How to warm up before exercising

exercises.name: Neck Rotation
instructions: Sit upright with your shoulders relaxed and down.
Turn your head slowly toward one shoulder as far as is comfortable.
Hold for a few seconds and return to the centre.
Repeat to the other side, three times each way.
exercises.commonMistakes: Forcing the range or letting the shoulders turn with the head.
exercises.beginnerModification: Turn through a smaller range.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It keeps the neck moving freely, which helps with tasks like checking over your shoulder.

exercises.name: Neck Side Stretch
instructions: Sit upright and look straight ahead.
Hold one shoulder down with the opposite hand.
Slowly tilt your head away from that shoulder until you feel a gentle stretch.
Hold for a few seconds, return to the centre, and repeat on the other side.
exercises.formCue: Ear toward shoulder, shoulder stays down.
exercises.commonMistakes: Pulling on the head or letting the held shoulder hike up.
exercises.beginnerModification: Tilt only a little and skip the shoulder hold.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It eases the side of the neck after long periods of sitting.

exercises.name: Standing Toe Raise
instructions: Stand tall holding a support with feet hip-width apart.
Rock back gently onto your heels and lift the fronts of both feet.
Keep your knees soft and your hips over your heels.
Lower the toes slowly and repeat.
exercises.formCue: Toes to shins, hips stay stacked.
exercises.commonMistakes: Sticking the hips back or leaning on the support.
exercises.beginnerModification: Do it seated, lifting the toes with heels on the floor.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Strong shin muscles lift the toes clear of the ground with each step.

source.name: Otago Exercise Programme (Royal Orthopaedic Hospital NHS)

exercises.name: Heel Walk
instructions: Stand tall beside a counter or rail.
Lift your toes so your weight is on your heels.
Walk 10 small steps on your heels, looking ahead.
Lower your feet, turn around, and walk back the same way.
exercises.commonMistakes: Bending forward at the hips or taking long strides.
exercises.beginnerModification: Keep a hand on the support the whole way.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It combines shin strength with balance in a walking pattern.

source.name: Otago Exercise Programme (Royal Orthopaedic Hospital NHS)

exercises.name: Ankle Alphabet
exercises.musclesWorked: Ankle joint, calf and shin muscles
instructions: Sit on a chair or bench high enough that one foot can hang free.
Lead with the big toe and trace the letters of the alphabet in the air.
Keep the movement small and coming from the ankle, not the knee or hip.
Finish the alphabet, then switch feet.
exercises.formCue: Draw with the big toe. Shin stays still.
exercises.commonMistakes: Moving the whole leg instead of the ankle.
exercises.beginnerModification: Trace half the alphabet, or just point and pull the foot ten times.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It takes the ankle through every direction it moves, which helps keep it mobile.

source.name: AAOS OrthoInfo, Foot and Ankle Conditioning Program

exercises.name: Foot Arch Roll
exercises.equipment: Golf ball or small massage ball, chair
instructions: Sit on a stable chair with both feet on the floor.
Place a small ball under the arch of one foot.
Roll the ball slowly back and forth from heel to ball of the foot for up to two minutes.
Switch feet.
exercises.commonMistakes: Standing on the ball with full weight.
exercises.beginnerModification: Use a softer or larger ball.
exercises.whyThisMatters: A short roll under the arch can make the feet feel looser after a long day standing.

source.name: AAOS OrthoInfo, Foot and Ankle Conditioning Program
